ai.title: Paediatric Congestive Cardiac Failure
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Paediatric heart failure occurs when cardiac output cannot meet the metabolic demands of the body. In resource-limited settings, it is driven by congenital defects, severe anaemia, and acquired infections like rheumatic heart disease. Prompt recognition relies on bedside signs: tachypnoea, hepatomegaly, gallop rhythm, and cardiomegaly.

sections.p: A clinical syndrome where the heart cannot pump sufficient blood to support tissue metabolism at normal filling pressures. Bedside clinical diagnosis relies on detecting key signs of systemic and pulmonary congestion.
b: Tachypnoea (often with subcostal recession and head nodding in infants)
Tachycardia out of proportion to fever or crying
Tender hepatomegaly from systemic venous congestion
Cardiomegaly demonstrated by displaced apex beat or chest radiography
Third heart sound (gallop rhythm) indicating ventricular volume overload

sections.p: Staged clinically using the modified Ross Heart Failure Classification for children.
b: Class I: Asymptomatic with normal feeding and growth
Class II: Mild tachypnoea or diaphoresis with feeds in infants; dyspnoea on exertion in older children
Class III: Marked tachypnoea or sweating with feeds, prolonged feeding times, and poor growth
Class IV: Symptomatic at rest with tachypnoea, retractions, grunting, or diaphoresis

sections.p: Causes vary markedly by age and epidemiological setting, with infection and severe nutritional anaemia dominating low-resource contexts alongside structural disease.
b: Infants: Congenital heart disease with left-to-right shunts (large VSD, PDA, AVSD) typically presenting at 4 to 8 weeks
Infants: Obstructive lesions (coarctation of the aorta, critical aortic stenosis)
Any age: Severe nutritional or malarial anaemia causing high-output failure
Children: Rheumatic heart disease (severe mitral or aortic regurgitation)
Children: Infective endocarditis (presents with explosive failure, fever, and new murmurs)
Infectious myocarditis (viral pathogens, HIV-associated cardiomyopathy)
Tuberculous or purulent pericardial effusion causing tamponade
Acute glomerulonephritis presenting with fluid overload and hypertension

sections.p: Presentation differs by developmental stage. Infants show systemic feeding difficulties, while older children report exercise limitation.
b: Infants: Poor feeding, stopping feeds to breathe, excessive forehead diaphoresis during feeding
Infants: Failure to thrive and faltering weight gain
Children: Fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and abdominal pain from hepatic stretching
Tachycardia and tachypnoea at rest
Hepatomegaly with a rounded, tender liver edge
Raised jugular venous pressure or prominent neck veins in older children
Peripheral oedema is late and uncommon in infants compared to adults

sections.p: Investigations confirm the syndrome, assess severity, and identify reversible triggers, tailored to resource availability.

t.b: Answers if cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion exist; shows cardiothoracic ratio greater than 0.60 in infants or 0.50 in older children, with pulmonary plethora or oedema
Identifies severe anaemia precipitating high-output failure or underlying bacterial infection/leukocytosis
Confirms structural defects, valve dysfunction, shunt direction, and contractility; when unavailable, manage empirically based on clinical exam and chest radiography
Detects hypoglycaemia in exhausted infants and baseline potassium/sodium prior to initiating diuretic therapy
Assesses for acute glomerulonephritis (haematuria, proteinuria, red cell casts) driving fluid retention
Identifies bloodstream organisms if infective endocarditis or severe systemic sepsis is suspected with new murmurs
Detects chamber enlargement, ventricular hypertrophy, ischaemia, or arrhythmias driving or complicating failure

sections.p: Critical decompensation demands emergency intervention to prevent arrest.
b: Cardiogenic shock: cold peripheries, prolonged capillary refill time, weak thready pulses, hypotension
Altered mental status, lethargy, or extreme irritability due to poor cerebral perfusion
Severe respiratory distress with central cyanosis, grunting, and frothy blood-stained sputum
Acute severe arrhythmias precipitating sudden collapse
Marked oliguria or anuria indicating end-organ renal hypoperfusion

sections.p: Treatment balances immediate stabilization, preload and afterload reduction, and correcting underlying precipitating causes.
b: Position child upright or at 45 degrees to reduce venous return and optimize diaphragm excursion
Give supplemental oxygen only if hypoxaemic (SpO2 under 90%); avoid hyperoxia in duct-dependent congenital lesions
Loop diuretics: furosemide administered to rapidly decrease preload and relieve pulmonary congestion
Aldosterone antagonists: spironolactone added for neurohormonal blockade and potassium preservation
ACE inhibitors: captopril or enalapril introduced to reduce afterload once haemodynamically stable; monitor renal function and potassium
Inotropic support: dopamine or dobutamine in intensive care for cardiogenic shock and low perfusion
Digoxin: reserved for selected myocardial failure or supraventricular arrhythmias; avoid in acute myocarditis due to ventricular arrhythmia risk
Supportive nutrition: high-calorie feeds via nasogastric tube to avoid feeding fatigue; do not restrict breastfeeding
Treat underlying causes: cautious blood transfusion for severe anaemia (slowly with concurrent furosemide), antibiotics for endocarditis

sections.p: Long-term monitoring focuses on growth, symptom stability, and secondary prophylaxis.
b: Serial weight monitoring to detect both fluid retention and nutritional recovery
Titration of heart failure pharmacotherapy as the child grows
Benzathine penicillin G prophylaxis every 3 to 4 weeks for rheumatic heart disease
Early surgical or catheter repair referral for structural congenital heart lesions
Routine immunization including pneumococcal, influenza, and measles vaccines

sections.p: Distinguishing cardiac disease from common tropical and respiratory conditions is critical.
b: Severe pneumonia: Both cause tachypnoea and chest indrawing; pneumonia lacks cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly, features crackles with fever, and lacks gallop rhythm
Severe malnutrition (Kwashiorkor): Peripheral oedema and hepatomegaly occur; heart is small rather than enlarged unless fluid-overloaded
Severe bronchial asthma or bronchiolitis: Expiratory wheeze dominates; liver may be pushed down by hyperinflated lungs but is not congested
Septic shock: Warm or cold extremities and tachycardia; lacks elevated venous pressures unless complicated by acute myocardial depression

sections.p: Recognise physiological and technical nuances that lead to diagnostic errors.
b: Chest X-ray: Thymic shadow in infants mimics cardiomegaly; poor inspiratory effort exaggerates cardiac size and bronchovascular markings
Liver palpation: Hyperinflated lungs in bronchiolitis displace the liver downwards without true enlargement; look for liver span and softness
Peripheral oedema: Often absent in infants with severe heart failure; its absence does not rule out CCF
Murmurs: Can be absent in severe failure with low flow, or innocent flow murmurs can be magnified by fever and severe anaemia

whenToSeekHelp: Severe difficulty breathing, chest indrawing, or grunting at rest
Refusal to feed or sweating profusely while attempting to feed
Bluish discoloration of the lips or tongue (central cyanosis)
Cold hands and feet with delayed capillary refill
Sudden swelling of the face, abdomen, or lower limbs

faq.q: Why is peripheral oedema rare in infants with heart failure?
faq.a: Infants have higher vascular compliance and lower tissue turgor; congestion manifests primarily as hepatomegaly and pulmonary fluid rather than dependent leg oedema.

faq.q: Should a mother stop breastfeeding an infant in heart failure?
faq.a: No, breastfeeding should continue. Feeds may be divided into smaller, more frequent amounts, or supplemented via nasogastric tube to prevent fatigue.

faq.q: Why must blood transfusion be given slowly with a diuretic in severe anaemia with failure?
faq.a: Rapid volume expansion in a decompensated heart can precipitate fatal pulmonary oedema. Packed cells must be transfused slowly alongside furosemide.

exam: A 6-week-old infant presents with tachypnoea, poor feeding, and a soft systolic murmur. What is the most likely structural diagnosis and timing rationale? — Large left-to-right shunt (such as VSD); symptoms manifest at 4 to 8 weeks as physiological pulmonary vascular resistance drops, increasing left-to-right shunting.

How do you distinguish an anatomically enlarged liver from one displaced by hyperinflated lungs? — Percuss the upper liver border to measure total liver span; in hyperinflation the span is normal but the border is low, whereas in CCF the span is increased with a tender, rounded edge.

Why should oxygen be used with caution in a neonate with suspected duct-dependent congenital heart disease? — Oxygen is a potent pulmonary vasodilator and stimulates ductus arteriosus constriction, which can precipitate circulatory collapse in duct-dependent systemic or pulmonary flow.

An infant in congestive failure has severe nutritional anaemia (Hb 3 g/dL). What is the emergency management strategy? — High-output failure requires very slow packed red cell transfusion with concurrent IV furosemide to prevent worsening volume overload and acute pulmonary oedema.

Why are ACE inhibitors contraindicated in acute, unstable decompensated heart failure? — Initiating an ACE inhibitor during hypovolaemic or unstable decompensation causes profound hypotension and can precipitate acute kidney injury.

A child with rheumatic heart disease develops acute worsening failure, fever, and a changing murmur. What must be ruled out immediately? — Infective endocarditis; requires immediate blood cultures before starting empirical targeted intravenous antibiotic therapy.

What is the clinical significance of a third heart sound (S3 gallop) in an infant with respiratory distress? — It indicates rapid passive ventricular filling into a non-compliant or volume-overloaded ventricle, confirming a cardiac rather than primary pulmonary cause of distress.
